title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLVII
paragraphs:
Was never true love loved in vain,
For truest love is highest gain.
No art can make it: it must spring
Where elements are fostering.
So in heaven’s spot and hour
Springs the little native flower,
Downward root and upward eye,
Shapen by the earth and sky.

Will Ladislaw’s little argument with Lydgate took place on a Saturday evening. Back in his rooms, he sat up half the night, freshly irritated, reconsidering everything he had already thought about settling in Middlemarch and attaching himself to Mr. Brooke. His earlier doubts about taking that step had become a sensitivity to any suggestion that he should not have taken it. That explained his anger with Lydgate, an anger that still left him restless. Was he making a fool of himself, just when he felt more certain than ever that he was better than a fool? And for what purpose?

Well, for no definite purpose. He did have dreamy visions of possibilities. Nobody who possesses both feelings and thoughts fails to think under the influence of those feelings, to see images rise that soothe passion with hope or sting it with fear. But this universal experience varies widely. Will was not one of those whose intelligence stayed on the main road. He followed byways where he found small pleasures of his own choosing, pleasures that gentlemen cantering along the highway might consider idiotic. The happiness he made for himself out of his feeling for Dorothea was one example. Strange as it may seem, Mr. Casaubon’s ordinary, vulgar suspicion had no power to tempt or absorb him: the prospect that Dorothea might become a widow, and that her interest in him might lead her to accept him as a husband. He did not inhabit that imagined scene and follow it through as we all follow the alternative life that serves as our practical heaven. It was not simply that he refused thoughts open to an accusation of baseness, or that he already felt uneasy about having to defend himself against a charge of ingratitude. An underlying awareness of the many barriers besides her husband that separated him from Dorothea also turned his imagination away from speculating about Mr. Casaubon’s fate. There were other reasons too. As we know, Will could not bear the idea of a flaw in his crystal. The calm freedom with which Dorothea looked at him and spoke both delighted and exasperated him. Thinking of her exactly as she was gave such exquisite pleasure that he could not wish for a change which would somehow change her. Do we not avoid a fine melody reduced to a street tune? Do we not recoil on learning that a rarity—perhaps a carving or engraving, which we have contemplated with even greater delight because of the trouble required to glimpse it—is actually quite common and available for everyday ownership? Our good depends on the quality and breadth of our feelings. Will cared little for life’s supposedly solid goods and greatly for its subtler influences. To carry within him such a feeling for Dorothea was like inheriting a fortune. What others might call the futility of his passion gave his imagination further delight. He felt an impulse of generosity, and found in his own experience the higher love poetry that had charmed his fancy. Dorothea, he told himself, sat enthroned for ever in his soul. No other woman could rise higher than her footstool. Had he been able to describe her effect on him in immortal verse, he might have boasted, like old Drayton, that:

“Queens in years to come might gladly live
On scraps of praise too plentiful for her.”

But that achievement was uncertain. What else could he do for Dorothea? What value did his devotion have for her? He could not tell. He would not move beyond her reach. Among her friends he saw nobody to whom he could imagine her speaking with the same simple confidence she showed him. She had once said she would like him to stay. Stay he would, whatever fire-breathing dragons hissed around her.

That was always where his doubts ended. Yet he could contradict and rebel even against his own decision. Often, as on this particular night, some outward sign irritated him by showing that his public work under Mr. Brooke’s leadership could never look as heroic as he wished. This irritation always joined another: despite sacrificing his dignity for Dorothea, he hardly ever saw her. Unable to dispute those unpleasant facts, he disputed his own strongest inclination instead and said, “I’m a fool.”

Nevertheless, because the whole inward debate revolved around Dorothea, it ended as before by sharpening his sense of what her presence would mean to him. Suddenly remembering that tomorrow was Sunday, he decided to go to Lowick Church and see her. He went to sleep with that intention. But while he dressed in the rational morning light, Objection spoke:
“That would practically defy Mr. Casaubon’s ban on visiting Lowick. Dorothea will be displeased.”
“Nonsense!” Inclination replied. “It would be outrageous for him to stop me visiting a pretty country church on a spring morning. And Dorothea will be pleased.”
“Mr. Casaubon will know perfectly well that you’ve come either to irritate him or to see Dorothea.”

“I’m not going to irritate him. And why shouldn’t I see Dorothea? Must he have everything to himself and be comfortable all the time? Let him suffer a little, like everyone else. I’ve always liked the quaint church and congregation. Besides, I know the Tuckers. I’ll sit in their pew.”

Having silenced Objection by sheer unreason, Will walked towards Lowick as if bound for Paradise. He crossed Halsell Common and skirted the wood, where broad sunlight shone beneath budding branches, revealing the beauty of moss and lichen and new green growth pushing through the brown. Everything seemed aware it was Sunday and approved his churchgoing. Will found happiness easy when nothing crossed his wishes. By now the thought of annoying Mr. Casaubon had become rather amusing. It brought out his merry smile, as pleasant to watch as sunlight breaking over water, though its cause was not admirable. Most of us, however, readily decide that anyone blocking our path is hateful. We do not mind giving him a little of the disgust his personality creates in us. Will walked with a small book under his arm and a hand in each side pocket. He never read, but sang a little while imagining scenes inside the church and on leaving it. He was testing tunes for some words of his own, sometimes borrowing an existing melody, sometimes inventing one. The words were not exactly a hymn, but they certainly suited his Sunday experience:

“O me, O me, what frugal cheer
My love doth feed upon!
A touch, a ray, that is not here,
A shadow that is gone:

“A dream of breath that might be near,
An inly-echoed tone,
The thought that one may think me dear,
The place where one was known,

“The tremor of a banished fear,
An ill that was not done—
O me, O me, what frugal cheer
My love doth feed upon!”

Sometimes he took off his hat and tossed his head back as he sang, showing his delicate throat. Then he looked like spring itself made flesh, its spirit filling the air: a radiant creature rich in uncertain promises.

The bells were still ringing when he reached Lowick. He entered the curate’s pew before anyone else arrived. Yet after the congregation had assembled, he remained alone there. The pew faced the rector’s at the entrance to the small chancel. Looking around at the country faces, Will had time to fear that Dorothea would not come. Year after year this congregation gathered between the whitewashed walls and dark old pews with scarcely more change than the branches of a tree, some breaking with age while others put out shoots. Mr. Rigg’s frog-like face was an alien, inexplicable addition. Despite that disturbance in the natural order, the Waules and country Powderells still sat side by side in their pews. Brother Samuel’s cheeks were as round and purple as ever. Three generations of respectable cottagers came as before, conscious of their duty towards their social superiors in general. The youngest children probably regarded Mr. Casaubon, in his black gown and highest pulpit, as the chief of all their betters and the most terrible to offend. Even in 1831 Lowick was peaceful, stirred no more by Reform than by the Sunday sermon’s solemn course. The congregation remembered Will’s earlier appearances and scarcely noticed him, except for the choir, who expected him to make himself heard in the singing.

At last Dorothea appeared against this quaint background. She walked up the short aisle wearing her white beaver-fur bonnet and gray cloak, the same ones she had worn in the Vatican. Since she faced the chancel as she entered, even her short-sighted eyes soon recognized Will. Outwardly she showed her feelings only by growing a little pale and giving him a solemn bow as she passed. To his surprise, he suddenly felt uneasy. After returning her bow, he dared not look at her again. Two minutes later Mr. Casaubon came out of the vestry and sat in the pew facing her, completing Will’s paralysis. He could look nowhere but towards the choir in the little gallery above the vestry door. Perhaps Dorothea was distressed; he had made a dreadful mistake. Annoying Casaubon was no longer amusing. Mr. Casaubon probably had the advantage of watching him and seeing that he dared not turn his head. Why had he not imagined this? Yet he could hardly have expected to sit alone in that square pew without the Tuckers to relieve him. Apparently they had left Lowick altogether, for a new clergyman occupied the reading desk. Still, he now called himself stupid for failing to foresee that he could not possibly look towards Dorothea, and that she might even think his visit impertinent. There was no escaping his cage. He found the places in his book and studied it like a schoolmistress. Never had morning service seemed so endlessly long. He felt utterly ridiculous, miserable and ill-tempered. This was the reward for worshipping the sight of a woman! The parish clerk noticed with surprise that Mr. Ladislaw did not join in the tune of Hanover, and supposed he might have a cold.

Mr. Casaubon did not preach that morning. Will’s situation remained unchanged until the blessing was pronounced and everyone rose. At Lowick, custom allowed “the betters” to leave first. Suddenly determined to break the spell over him, Will looked straight at Mr. Casaubon. But Casaubon’s eyes were fixed on the pew-door latch. He opened it, let Dorothea pass and followed immediately without looking up. As she turned out of the pew, Will caught her eye. Again she bowed, this time looking agitated, as though holding back tears. He followed them outside, but they went straight towards the little gate from the churchyard into the shrubbery without turning round.
He could not follow them. All he could do was walk sadly home at midday along the road he had traveled so hopefully that morning. Both around him and within him, the light had entirely changed.
